extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and practitioners (physiologists, meteorologists, literary scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying physiological and observational criteria for identifying and characterizing hypnotic states (as presented in a lecture-essay), together with related meteorological measurement standards and aesthetic-evolution observations appearing on the same page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete loss of consciousness (essential symptom)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the essential symptoms of the hypnotic sleep is the more or less complete loss of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only in a complete state of hypnotism do persons subjected to the experiment preserve a remembrance of what has passed during their sleep; in lighter states memory may be only suspended and can sometimes be revived by associative cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensorial perceptions without conscious representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensorial perceptions take place even in the most complete hypnotism, but the power of transforming them into conscious representations, and consequently of fixing them in the memory, is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypnotics may perceive sensations unconsciously (analogous to waking persons whose attention is elsewhere); such perceptions can later be recalled only if not effaced by later impressions and sometimes require associative cues to revive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention as requirement for consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate affection of the senses and conscious perception are distinct physiological conditions, the latter of which supposes a holding of the attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of attention explains how hypnotics can perceive stimuli yet fail to form conscious memories; attention must be controlled when testing awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious perception leading to involuntary imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements perceived unconsciously, by the aid of the sight or hearing, are imitated by the hypnotic involuntarily and under a constraint from which he cannot withdraw himself, and with an almost servile exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypnotics will regulate steps, raise arms, bend body to match the experimenter; even with eyes shut (eyelids not wholly closed) they can imitate observed movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of suggestive pre-presentation for induced acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypnotic can be made to execute movements of which the sensation has been communicated to them in advance; the operator gives an order which the hypnotic does not apprehend but which he executes if he has unconsciously experienced a corresponding sensorial impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates mechanism of 'magnetizer' control; implies careful control of pre-exposure when designing experiments or tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing memory without suggestion (avoid leading questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In testing whether the hypnotic, after waking, remembers what has passed, it is important that he be not assisted by being asked a question the form of which will suggest the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asked a leading question the subject will often answer 'Yes'; better to ask open questions like 'what has taken place' to get an unprompted report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of hypnotism and corresponding symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: In a slight degree of hypnotism the sensoria commune is still so free that the constraint of involuntary imitation does not exist; as consciousness is more obscured, sensorial excitation predominates producing involuntary acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a graded progression: slight (little imitation), deeper (unconscious perception causes action), very deep (all traces of sensorial perceptions disappear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Painlessness as advanced symptom
rubrics_metrics.description: A more advanced symptom of hypnotism is painlessness. Sensibility returns with the cessation of the sleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analgesia during hypnotic state is diagnostic but temporary; check return of sensation after waking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and prolonged reflex excitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The exaggeration of the reflex excitation of the striated muscles is striking and of surprising duration; a person who has been hypnotized preserves the reflex irritability for whole days and weeks after returning to normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for heightened reflex responses post-hypnosis and note duration; this may be used as evidence of prior hypnotic state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localized tactile excitation induces graded motor contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: By passing the finger several times over the fleshy part of the thumb we may cause it to bend toward the palm; stronger excitation brings more distant muscle groups into play and prolonged excitation can extend contraction across limbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a method to evoke and map motor responses during hypnotism: start with light rubbing of thumb, increase intensity to engage forearm, elbow, shoulder, then contralateral limbs; pause before respiratory muscles are affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe limits and precautions for motor-excitation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Great prudence is necessary lest experiments be carried too far and the respiratory muscles be affected. Rigidity may become extreme so that respiratory function could be endangered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pause when contraction becomes extensive; use slight shock or quickly opening fingers of a closed hand to stop contraction; never allow respiratory muscles to be compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical rigidity demonstration (plank-like stiffness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscles may be so rigid in robust persons that the body is stiff as a plank; it is possible to rest a hypnotic by head and feet on two chairs and carry him around without his body bending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extreme rigidity is both diagnostic and potentially hazardous; treat with care and supervise removal of such rigidity safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eyelids not wholly closed; perception persists
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypnotic, although his eyes are shut, perceives what is passing around him. The eyelids are not wholly closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume absence of visual input simply because eyes are shut; consider partial visual perception when interpreting responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between unconscious perception and conscious recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensorial impressions which do not excite consciousness give way to movements accomplished almost without control; later, slight allusions may revive memory traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interviewing post-hypnotic subjects, use neutral prompts to elicit memory without leading; recognition that unconscious traces can be reactivated by cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect meteorological records to trace storm progression
rubrics_metrics.description: What is chiefly demanded is the collection of such meteorological records and observations as may render it possible to trace completely the rise, progress, and varying intensity of the storm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble barometer, anemograph, rain-gauge, and direction records across the affected region; accept that time and more observations are needed for complete analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barometric fall as indicator of storm approach and intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a steady fall in the barometer up to the time of maximum violence of the wind; the minimum observed height and range over time are diagnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chart barometric curve (showing actual vertical movement) and note minima and range; compare with historic ranges for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and frequent recording (hourly/half-hourly) of barometer and anemograph
rubrics_metrics.description: Before 1 a.m. only three observations were recorded; after 1 a.m. observations were made hourly and during a considerable portion of the time half-hourly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High temporal resolution is crucial: gaps can hide sudden falls/rises; strive for continuous registers to capture peaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anemographs and verification against secondary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocities are computed from a continuous record made by an anemograph consisting of a Robinson's anemometer with Beckley's registering apparatus attached; smaller anemometer used as a check showed the registering instrument may overestimate very high winds and underestimate low speeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check instruments when possible; be aware of instrument-specific biases and possible mechanical stoppage (pendulum arrest) during extreme blasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record wind direction continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous record of the direction of the wind is kept; during the period considered direction varied between north and west with notable shifts between two and three o'clock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction changes are diagnostically important; maintain uninterrupted directional logs alongside velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rain-gauge readings for total rainfall
rubrics_metrics.description: Rain-gauges emptied at 7 a.m. showed a total of 4.66 inches, nearly all of which must have fallen during at most two or three hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent emptying/readings after violent rainfall are necessary to estimate short-duration intense precipitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for recording interruptions and likely unrecorded maxima
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to interruption in the continuity of records it is impossible to affirm that the maximum velocity was recorded; evidence (stopped anemograph pendulum, destroyed small anemometer) suggests greater peaks occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always evaluate possible unrecorded peaks when instruments fail during extreme events; corroborate with witness testimony and secondary damage indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert wind velocity to pressure using square-law assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally assumed that the pressure is proportional to the square of the velocity; on a scale adopted by Smithsonian and US Signal Service, velocity of 25 mph corresponds to ~3 pounds per square foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the velocity^2 law to estimate wind pressure; compare to engineering standards to assess structural risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering standards for wind pressure and factor of safety
rubrics_metrics.description: French and many English engineers have adopted fifty-five pounds per square foot as a standard, and about the same number is used in America, but it seems doubtful if even that furnishes a sufficient 'factor of safety.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed or estimated pressures against adopted standards (e.g., 50–55 lb/ft^2) and consider whether higher safety factors are warranted in design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation for national signal/observation service
rubrics_metrics.description: Had an efficient system of observations, telegrams, and signals existed, timely warning might have been given of its approach, and possibly much property and many lives saved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for an efficient and complete signal service for the benefit of the whole country; coordinate observation networks and communication channels for warnings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of aesthetic evolution (human to abstract beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic faculty progressed from simple admiration of human beauty, to works of primitive art, to admiration of fern tracery and shells, and lastly to love of rocks, hills, seas, and clouds for their intrinsic loveliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this historical sequence to analyze or evaluate the aesthetic emphasis in a culture or period: check which classes of objects are valued (human form, crafted objects, small natural forms, large-scale scenery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropinistic early stage: focus on human beauty and artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry at first is all epic or narrative; initial aesthetic feeling attaches primarily to the human face and figure and the works of man's primitive art; nature is often only alluded to as a difficulty to be overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying early or less-cultivated tastes, expect priority given to human-centered beauty and socially salient artifacts rather than landscapes or scenery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor components of scenery (color) are early accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor component elements of scenery (bright color in flowers, gems, rainbow, sunset clouds) must always have been beautiful even to children and savages, though remote from personal interest they would be little regarded by primitive mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between primitive appreciation of isolated visual qualities (color) and later developed appreciation for large-scale scenic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation and husbandry as catalysts for scenic taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When cultivation began, the care of the husbandman and the aesthetic interest aroused by his regular neatness (straight rows of vines, trim meadows, well-kept hedges, level fields of corn) naturally set up a new feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether appreciation of landscapes is linked to agricultural neatness and human-managed scenes; cultural and economic conditions (roads, travel, security) mediate development of taste for scenery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel, security, and improved communication foster scenic appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: With greater security and easier travel, mountains and forests and waterfalls became more easy to visit; the habit of making tours spreading to middle classes has had an immense effect in strengthening the love of nature; railways increased comparative observation and admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the role of mobility and exposure: access and comparative exposure grow capacity to appreciate subtler scenic forms; infrastructural improvements can expand aesthetic sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation is socially and racially variable
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste for scenery on a large scale is confined to comparatively few races and comparatively few persons among them (examples: Chinese and Hindoos care little for landscape; Russians 'run through Europe with carriage-windows shut'; many Americans prefer cultivated flat landscape).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing aesthetic response across cultures, account for differing emphases (urban vs rural values, utility-based valuation) and avoid assuming universality of scenic preference.
